contact_edits.before: This is altogether a lighter production than the original. (Lighter in the most basic sense--it is, if I can trust my memory, far more brightly lit.) This has something to do with time, something probably with the logical French language and the ironic French temperament. But, if the delivery is light, it carries a heavy freight. Konga, dreaming awkwardly of his future, has wonderful moments of delicate comedy, pipe in his mouth, assuming a manager's pose. The photography theme is constant and vital to the plot. It's a service that Styles, reflecting on early ghastly experiences with family groups ("37 New Brighton smiles on the same photo--never again") has, without knowing it, been setting himself up as a saviour. Habib Dembele gives him a joyous, elfin quality and balances it with good-humoured man-of-the-world exasperation as Sizwe's friend and other rescuer, the man who exhorts him to grab at salvation, even when he finds it literally lying in the gutter. Between them, these actors create a world for us. The play is little like Fugard's unaided works, which are drier and also duller; it's full of pungent detail, shrugged or mocked at, understated to shock. Dembele plays several roles, Konga only one, but they both give the impression of enormous versatility and enormous mutual trust. The level of contact here--actor to actor, actors to audience -- is remarkable. Brook, in the simplest way, has done it again. - Until April 22. Call 416-973-4000 for ticket information.
